summary: This report reviews the key features of RIP version 2 and the implementation experience gained so far, as the routing protocol criteria of RFC 1264 required before a protocol advances. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1721.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a new rule for sharing road maps between routers could move forward, someone had to check what it does and whether it worked in practice. This paper is that check-up.

questions: how does rip-2 improve on rip
subtitle: An assessment of RIP-2 protocol features and early implementation results.

tldr.problem: The IETF had developed RIP version 2 to fix limitations of the original RIP protocol, and needed to evaluate whether it worked in practice before standardizing it.
tldr.mechanism: This informational RFC reviews the key improvements RIP-2 offers (routing domains, external tags, subnet masks, next-hop support, authentication, multicasting) and documents implementation experience with the protocol.
tldr.outcome: The evaluation showed RIP-2 was implementable with multiple working versions. It became a Proposed Standard and is still used as a distance-vector routing protocol for small networks.

facts.label: New features
facts.value: 6: domains, tags, masks, next-hop, auth, multicast

today: RFC 1387 is Informational and was made obsolete by RFC 1721. RIP-2 has been widely implemented and remains in use as a distance-vector routing protocol, particularly in small networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RIP version 2 extends the original Routing Information Protocol (RIP-1) from RFC 1058 with new features to make it more flexible and powerful. RFC 1388 defines the protocol itself, and RFC 1389 defines its MIB (management interface). RFC 1387 provides this analysis as required by the Routing Protocol Criteria (RFC 1264).

The analysis documents RIP-2's new capabilities and the implementation experience gained during development, serving as the technical review needed for protocol standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP is a way routers share route information with each other. A new version adds helpful features. Before it could become official, someone had to check if it really works.

sections.title: Key Features of RIP-2
sections.content: RIP-2 adds six major improvements to RIP-1. Routing domains allow multiple independent RIP clouds to exist on the same physical network, enabling simple policy-based router grouping. External route tags carry information from other routing protocols (for example, AS numbers from BGP). Subnet masks allow variable-length masks, necessary for classless addressing (CIDR). Next-hop addresses let a router indicate better routes through other routers when multiple protocols are in use. Authentication protects RIP messages with passwords (extensible for stronger schemes). Multicasting reduces load on non-routing hosts by sending RIP packets to a multicast address instead of broadcasting to all.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP-2 adds six things: separate groups of routers, tags from other systems, flexible network masks, better path hints, password protection, and quieter messages. Each one solves a real problem from the original RIP.

sections.title: Implementation Experience
sections.content:
At the time of publication, one nearly complete implementation existed: gated, written by Jeffrey Honig at Cornell University. It supported multicasting, subnet masks, limited authentication, next-hop, and limited routing domain support, with RIP-2 tools like ripquery available. The gated implementation had been tested against itself and RIP-1 implementations, though full support for subsumption rules, complete authentication, complete routing domains, and the MIB was still being developed.

A second complete implementation was under development by a vendor whose identity could not be disclosed at that time. This demonstrated that RIP-2 was implementable despite its added complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Two companies were building RIP-2. One version (gated) was mostly working and was tested. The second was still in progress. This proved the new protocol could actually be built.
